vignette:
Amara is a 42-year-old Congolese-born woman who came to the United States following a period of political detention in her home country. She is divorced, lives alone in a small apartment near the factory where she works the early morning shift, and presented for psychological evaluation with a PCL-5 score of 73. She described her reason for seeking help with characteristic understatement: she said she was "not functioning the way a person should."

The events that brought her to this point occurred approximately four years ago, when Amara was detained by security forces and held for eleven days. During that time she was subjected to prolonged physical torture in a concrete room that smelled of rust and damp earth. Her captors referred to her repeatedly by a shortened form of her name — a diminutive she had once loved — and the sessions often took place in the early morning hours during the region's heavy rainy season, the sound of downpours audible through a narrow window above her head. She was eventually released without explanation and made her way, over many months, to the United States.

Amara's memory of those eleven days carries a quality she struggles to articulate. She says the events were so extreme that she sometimes cannot believe they happened to her — they feel, she says, like something she read about rather than something she survived. The memory feels alien, as though it belongs to another woman entirely. And yet it is not distant: when the memory surfaces, she can smell the rust and the wet concrete as clearly as if she were standing in that room, and this sensory return is what she finds most destabilising. The vividness of that olfactory recall pulls her back into the memory with a force that overrides her sense of being safe in the present, and in the wake of such intrusions she finds herself scanning her apartment for sounds — listening at the door, tracking every creak of the building — certain that the danger the memory carries is somehow still real and proximate.

Her body, she has come to believe, cannot be trusted. It reacts before she has had time to think: she startles violently at ordinary sounds on the factory floor — a dropped metal casing, a compressed-air hiss — and her heart is already pounding before her mind has registered what she heard. This hypervigilant state, in which her body seems to operate on a threat logic of its own, has led her to a dark conclusion: that she is no longer capable of the things that once defined her. Before her detention, she was known among her family as someone physically strong, emotionally steady, dependable under pressure. Now she feels the world to be fundamentally dangerous, her body unreliable, and herself diminished. These appraisals are not abstract — they press on her daily, and they keep her oriented toward threat in a way that makes even ordinary moments feel precarious.

Certain things in her daily life function as doorways back into the room. Physical closeness — a supervisor leaning over her workstation, a colleague brushing past her in the corridor — produces an immediate somatic alarm. Hearing a name that resembles the diminutive her captors used causes her chest to tighten before she has consciously registered the sound. And when the weather turns heavy and humid, the way it does in late summer in this part of the Midwest, she finds herself unable to leave her apartment without effort, the air itself a trigger. When these moments arrive, the memory floods back with its smells and its weight, and the threat monitoring that was already running intensifies further — she listens harder, startles more readily, and her conviction that the world is dangerous and her body unreliable deepens.

To manage this, Amara has built a careful architecture of control. She applies heavy makeup each morning, covering the visible scars on her face and neck — wearing them exposed, she says, makes her feel like the woman in that room, not the woman at the machine. She avoids the clothes she was wearing during her detention, choosing her wardrobe with a precision her coworkers do not understand. She keeps her mind occupied at all times — podcasts during the commute, mental arithmetic during breaks — because stillness allows the memory to surface. But these strategies, she has begun to notice, are not working. The distraction keeps the memory just below the threshold of full recall without ever resolving it, and the avoidances have gradually narrowed her life: she has declined two promotions that would have required her to supervise others, certain she is no longer the capable person such a role would demand. What finally brought her to seek help was a morning last month when she heard a coworker's name called across the factory floor, smelled the industrial coolant that had pooled near her station, and found herself frozen at her machine for nearly four minutes, unable to move. What she most fears is that this will never stop tightening. What she most hopes is that someone can help her believe she is no longer in that room.

Aleksander Nowak is a 34-year-old firefighter of Polish descent who has been married for six years. He presents with a PCL-5 score of 40, seeking help for the first time after what he describes as months of feeling like he is "living behind glass" — present in his life but unable to fully inhabit it.

Several years ago, Aleksander volunteered through an international relief organization to spend three months supporting emergency medical and fire-response operations in an active conflict zone in Eastern Europe. He had gone in believing that his professional training would be sufficient preparation. It was not. The environment bore almost no resemblance to the structured incident command he knew from home. Buildings collapsed without warning. Convoys were redirected mid-route because roads had been shelled. Strangers — civilians, fighters, aid workers — moved through checkpoints in states of desperation or concealed intent that Aleksander could rarely read in time. On one afternoon that remains vivid to him, he was inside a partially destroyed administrative building coordinating a casualty evacuation when secondary shelling began. The stairwell he had entered through was blocked. He spent nearly forty minutes in a ground-floor corridor, methodically identifying every possible exit while the structure groaned above him, before he and two colleagues found a way out through a blown-out wall. No one was killed. But something shifted in him that afternoon that has not shifted back.

In the months following his return, Aleksander began organizing his environment in ways that felt, to him, entirely rational. He stopped exercising — the elevated heart rate and shortness of breath felt too close to what his body had done in that corridor, and he had come to associate those sensations with immediate danger. He made sure to position himself near exits in any room he entered: at the fire station, at restaurants, at his in-laws' home during Sunday dinners. He began scanning doorways and windows as a matter of reflex, cataloguing routes before he had even taken off his coat. What he understood less clearly was that these behaviors, rather than quieting the alarm, were feeding it. By treating every environment as a potential trap that required a pre-planned escape, Aleksander was continuously signaling to himself that the danger was real and present. The vigilance his strategies were meant to manage had become inseparable from them. His sense of threat had not diminished with time; it had been maintained, and in some respects amplified, by the very habits he had built to contain it.

He is alert inside his own home in a way that exhausts his wife, Marta. He sits facing the door. He notices when a neighbor's car parks differently than usual. When strangers approach him in ordinary settings — a man asking for directions outside the grocery store, a colleague's friend extending a hand at a barbecue — he experiences a spike of threat that he recognizes, intellectually, as disproportionate, but cannot override. At the fire station, where his occupation requires him to enter unfamiliar and structurally compromised buildings regularly, the scanning has become almost continuous. His crew has noticed that he insists on walking the perimeter of a structure before entering, even on calls where time does not comfortably permit it. He has not told them why.

Aleksander also pushes away positive emotions when they arise — moments of warmth with Marta, satisfaction after a successful call — because they feel, in some way he struggles to articulate, unsafe. As though allowing himself to feel well would mean lowering a guard he cannot afford to lower. This has cost him something in his marriage that both he and Marta are aware of but have not yet named directly.

What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last month when his seven-year-old nephew ran toward him unexpectedly in a hallway and Aleksander's body responded as though the child were a threat. He caught himself before reacting physically, but the look on his nephew's face stayed with him. He is most afraid, he says, that he has become someone his family needs to be careful around. What he is hoping for is to stop having to plan his escape from every room he walks into.

Valentina is a 47-year-old Salvadoran American woman who has been married for nineteen years and works as a social ministry worker at a Catholic community center in her city. She came to the intake session speaking quietly, her hands folded tightly in her lap, and described herself as someone who used to believe that helping others was the purpose that held her life together. That sense of purpose, she said, now feels like something she is only performing.

Approximately eight months ago, Valentina was raped by a man she had known professionally — a contractor who had been doing repair work at the community center. The assault occurred in the late afternoon, in a storage room at the back of the building, after the rest of the staff had left. What she remembers is not a continuous event but a series of frozen frames: the overhead light flickering, the sound of tools being set down on a metal shelf, the particular quality of silence that filled the room just before he moved toward her. That silence — thick, suspended, wrong — is the detail that has lodged most deeply in her nervous system. She has no fluid narrative of what happened. She told the clinician that she knows what occurred but cannot find the words to describe it, as though language itself has been revoked. When she tries to recall it, what surfaces are those still images, and with them, an immediate and overwhelming wave of guilt — a conviction that she should have left earlier, should have known, should have done something different.

Those guilt-saturated memories have fed directly into the beliefs that now organize her daily life. Valentina has come to feel that she deserves to suffer for what happened, a punishment logic she applies with quiet consistency. She restricts her eating carefully, finding in that control something that feels like the only domain in which she has agency. She avoids anything that would allow her body or mind to soften — rest, leisure, stillness — because relaxing feels to her not like safety but like exposure, like lowering a guard she cannot afford to lower. These strategies, in turn, have kept the memories from being processed in any narrative or integrated way; by never allowing herself to settle, she ensures that the frozen images remain exactly as they were, unexamined and uncontextualized, ready to resurface.

The memories also sustain a vigilance that has become exhausting. Valentina now experiences the silence of a room — any room, including the office where she meets with community members in need — as a signal that something dangerous is about to happen. When a colleague is late returning from lunch, or when a meeting runs past its scheduled time, she assumes something terrible is unfolding. She cannot relax even when she knows, intellectually, that she is safe. This chronic threat state has in turn reinforced her appraisals: she has concluded that the world is genuinely dangerous, that her perception of threat is accurate rather than distorted, and that she was foolish ever to have believed otherwise. The hypervigilance and the beliefs tighten around each other — the threat confirms the appraisals, and the appraisals confirm the threat — and her strategies of restriction and refusal to rest keep both elevated, preventing any disconfirmation from reaching her.

The appraisals themselves have become their own source of suffering. Valentina describes having lost her faith — in people, in the Church she served, in God — and says that the woman she was before, someone she remembers as genuinely happy, feels like a stranger. She carries a deep shame about what happened to her body, a shame she has not disclosed to her husband, who knows only that she has been "going through something." The distance this has created in their marriage is one of the concrete consequences she named: they no longer sleep easily beside each other, and she has declined every invitation to social gatherings their parish community organizes.

What finally brought Valentina to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago when she froze completely in the doorway of the storage room — now used by a different staff member — and could not move for several minutes. A colleague witnessed it. She is most afraid, she said, that she will never be able to do her work with full presence again. What she is hoping for, more quietly, is to find words for what happened.

Ernesto is a 70-year-old widowed dentist of Salvadoran descent who has practiced in the same modest clinic in a mid-sized American city for nearly three decades. He presented for psychological assessment after his daughter, alarmed by his increasing withdrawal and a recent incident at his clinic, persuaded him to seek help. His PCL-5 score of 42 places him in the moderate-to-severe range, and the picture that emerged across the intake and early sessions is one of a man quietly held hostage by an event that occurred more than forty years ago — and that, in his nervous system, has never fully ended.

Ernesto was in his late twenties, working as a young dental student in San Salvador, when a military patrol entered the university campus during a period of acute political violence. Without warning, shots were fired in the courtyard below his classroom window. He saw a fellow student fall. Uniformed soldiers moved through the corridor outside his door, and for what he describes as the longest minutes of his life, he pressed himself against the wall and did not move or call out. His friend died. Ernesto survived. He has never, in forty years, been able to construct a coherent verbal account of what happened — the event resists language entirely, existing instead as a set of sensory fragments: the crack of gunfire, the particular olive-green of the uniforms, the smell of concrete and blood. When the memory does surface, it does not feel like remembering. It feels like being there again, with full sensory immediacy, and the emotional force of it is so overwhelming that he has to physically stop whatever he is doing, grip the edge of his dental chair, and wait for it to pass. Because the memory is so resistant to narrative form, he has never been able to process or contextualize it, and this incompleteness has kept it perpetually raw.

In his daily work, Ernesto encounters his triggers with a regularity that has made the clinic itself a site of chronic low-grade dread. The clinic sits near a police substation, and officers occasionally walk past or enter the waiting room for routine dental appointments. The moment Ernesto sees a uniform — a police badge, a security guard's jacket, a patient who mentions military service — the memory fragments erupt without warning, dragging him back to that corridor. A car backfiring in the parking lot, or a patient dropping a metal instrument tray, produces the same effect: his body floods with alarm before his mind can intervene. These triggers do not merely distress him; they activate a state of acute threat, in which he begins scanning every room for exits the moment he enters it, watches patients' hands and postures for signs of danger, and holds himself in a state of sustained hypervigilance that leaves him exhausted by the end of each working day. The threat monitoring, in turn, keeps him in a physiological state in which almost anything can become a trigger — a raised voice in the waiting room, a patient who arrives in military fatigues — and the threshold for activation grows lower with each passing month.

To manage this, Ernesto has built a set of strategies that feel to him like reasonable precautions but that have steadily narrowed his life. He avoids all news coverage of Central American violence or anything involving armed conflict, and has stopped watching television almost entirely. He carries a licensed handgun in his coat pocket at all times, telling himself this is simply prudent for a man who works alone in a clinic. He ruminates extensively, returning again and again to the question of whether he could have done something to save his friend — whether his silence was cowardice, whether he is, at his core, a man who fails others when it matters. This self-blame, rather than resolving anything, keeps the memory activated and close to the surface, so that the next trigger finds him already primed. The weapon, the avoidance, the rumination — each of these strategies sustains the sense that the world remains dangerous, which sharpens his scanning and watchfulness, which ensures that triggers are encountered more frequently and responded to more intensely.

What finally brought him to the clinic was an afternoon when a patient arrived wearing a National Guard uniform. Ernesto excused himself, went to the back room, and sat on the floor for twenty minutes, unable to speak. He is afraid, he says quietly, that he is losing his mind. What he hopes for — though he does not quite believe it is possible — is a single day in which he does not feel like that young man still pressed against the wall, waiting for the door to open.

Marisol is a 47-year-old Salvadoran American woman who has been married for nineteen years and works as a social ministry worker at a Catholic community center in her city's largely immigrant neighborhood. She came to the clinic three months after being raped by a man she knew through her parish — a volunteer coordinator who had asked her to stay late one evening to review program materials. The attack happened in a small storage room off the main corridor, a room she had entered dozens of times before. What she remembers is not a continuous sequence but a series of frozen images: the overhead fluorescent light flickering once before he pushed her against the metal shelving, the particular silence of the building after the last staff member had left, the texture of a cardboard box against her shoulder. Each image is vivid and complete in itself, like a photograph, but the moments between them are gone. When she tries to speak about what happened — to her therapist, or in the single halting conversation she attempted with her husband — she finds that the words simply are not there. She knows what occurred. She cannot say it. What she can say, and has said more than once, is that she deserved it, that something she had done or failed to do had made this inevitable.

In the weeks after the assault, Marisol continued going to work. She had no language for what had happened and no framework that felt safe enough to hold it. She had spent twenty years organizing food drives, coordinating refugee resettlement, sitting with women in crisis, and she had come to believe, quietly and with gathering certainty, that she was now permanently separated from the person who had done that work. That woman had been happy, or something close to it. This woman was not. She had also lost something she could not easily name — a sense that the world was held together by something trustworthy, whether God or community or ordinary human decency. The faith that had been the foundation of both her vocation and her marriage now felt like a story she had told herself.

At the community center, the storage room remains off limits to her. She routes her path through the building to avoid it, which her colleagues have noticed without understanding. More disruptively, the silence that sometimes falls over the office — between phone calls, after a meeting ends — has become unbearable. That particular quality of quiet, the same quiet that preceded the attack, now registers in her body as warning. She will find a reason to speak, to move, to create noise. When a colleague is late returning from a home visit, Marisol's certainty that something terrible is happening mounts with each passing minute until she is calling the colleague's cell phone, her hands unsteady. Her supervisor has gently asked whether she is managing her caseload.

At home, Marisol has stopped eating dinner with her husband most evenings. She controls what she eats with a precision that she experiences as the one domain in which she remains competent and intact. She has also stopped allowing herself the ordinary comforts she once relied on — a bath in the evening, sitting still with a book — because stillness itself feels like exposure, like leaving a door unguarded. Her husband is confused and grieving the distance between them, though she has told him almost nothing. She had not found the words.

What finally brought her to the clinic was a moment at work when a teenage girl she was counseling described feeling that her body no longer belonged to her. Marisol recognized the sentence as her own. She made the appointment that afternoon. She arrives carrying a shame she has not been able to articulate — a deep conviction that what happened to her body has made her body wrong, contaminated in some way she cannot explain — and a fear that speaking will make everything worse rather than better. What she hopes for, tentatively, is to find the words. What she is most afraid of is that finding them will confirm what she already suspects: that she will not recover the person she was before that evening.

# Vignette: Hemi

Hemi is a 71-year-old Māori man who has been married to his wife, Aroha, for nearly forty-five years. He works part-time as a cashier at a large supermarket near his home in South Auckland — a job he took on after retiring from construction work, partly to stay busy, partly because he genuinely enjoys talking to people. Or he used to.

About two years ago, Hemi was finishing an evening shift when a young man entered the store and attacked another customer — a woman in her mid-thirties — with a knife, just three registers down from where Hemi was standing. He watched the whole thing unfold in the space of perhaps thirty seconds. He remembers the sound more than anything else: the woman's scream cutting off too quickly, the wet noise he cannot bring himself to describe even now, the way his own voice disappeared when he tried to call out. He was frozen behind his register, hands flat on the counter, unable to move until a colleague pulled him into the back room. The woman survived, but only just.

In the weeks that followed, Hemi told himself he was fine. He is not a man who has ever considered himself fragile. He went back to work after a few days, stood behind his register, and smiled at customers. But something had shifted in a way he could not name at the time. He began scanning every person who walked through the automatic doors — reading their hands, their body language, the shape of their jackets. If someone moved quickly or reached into a bag, his heart would slam against his ribs and he would find himself gripping the counter again, back in that moment, smelling the blood he is certain he could smell even from three registers away.

He stopped sleeping well almost immediately. He lies awake most nights running through what he should have done — shouted a warning, moved toward her, done *something* — even though he knows, on some level, that there was nothing to be done. When he does sleep, he wakes from dreams he cannot fully recall but that leave him drenched and rigid beside Aroha, who has learned not to touch him suddenly in the night.

Hemi has become quieter at home. His grandchildren visit on weekends, and he loves them fiercely, but he finds the noise and chaos of a full house overwhelming in a way it never used to be. He sits apart more often now, watching from the edges. Aroha has noticed. She is a patient woman, but she tells him she misses him — that he is present in the room but somewhere else entirely, and she doesn't know how to reach him.

At work, he has requested a register near the back of the store, away from the entrance. His manager accommodated this without asking questions, and Hemi is grateful for that small mercy. Still, there are days when a particular sound — a shopping basket dropped on the floor, a child shrieking with laughter — will send him somewhere he doesn't want to go, and he has to excuse himself to the stockroom and breathe until the world stops narrowing. He has not told his colleagues why.

He carries a particular kind of shame about all of this. He is a grandfather, a husband, a man who spent decades doing physical labor without complaint. He did not experience the trauma himself — he was not the one who was hurt — and this distinction matters enormously to him, even as it provides no relief. He finds himself thinking about the woman sometimes, wondering whether she still carries it too, whether she knows that a man three registers away has not stopped seeing her fall.

He came to therapy at Aroha's quiet insistence. He sat in the first session with his hands on his knees and said, carefully, that he wasn't sure he deserved to be there.

Malia Somsak is a 57-year-old Thai-American woman who has been married for thirty-one years and operates a small gift and import shop in a mid-sized Pacific Northwest city. She presented for psychological assessment approximately four months after what she describes, haltingly and with long pauses, as the worst period of her life — the sudden, near-fatal illness of her youngest son, then nineteen years old, who was admitted to the intensive care unit following a septic infection that went undetected for several days despite two prior visits to an urgent care clinic.

Malia had brought her son in twice before the hospitalization, each time describing his fever, his confusion, his strange pallor. Each time, she was told he likely had a viral illness and was sent home with instructions to rest and hydrate. On the third visit, he collapsed in the waiting room. What followed were eleven days in which Malia sat beside a hospital bed watching her son receive blood transfusions through IV lines, his arms mapped with bruising from repeated needle insertions, monitors tracking a body that seemed to be failing in real time. She held his hand while nurses adjusted drips and drew blood from his veins. She watched the bags of fluid and the tubing and the needles with the helpless attention of someone trying to understand a language she had never been taught. Her son survived, but the recovery was long, and Malia has not been the same since.

In the months that followed, she found herself unable to describe what had happened in any coherent way. When her husband or close friends asked how she was processing things, she would go quiet, not from reticence but because the words genuinely would not come — she knew what had occurred but could not assemble it into sentences. More disorienting still, she would sometimes be standing behind the counter of her shop, arranging ceramic figurines or counting receipts, and be overtaken by a wave of terror and grief so complete that it left her breathless, with no accompanying image, no clear memory surfacing — just the full weight of those eleven days pressing through her chest without explanation.

She had come to believe, with a certainty that felt immovable, that she had failed her son. The clinic had missed the signs twice, and she had accepted their reassurances and taken him home. She was certain she should have pushed harder, demanded more, refused to leave. Alongside this sat a fury she could not resolve: what happened was deeply unfair, and no one — not the clinic, not any administrator — had acknowledged it or been held accountable. This sense of institutional abandonment had calcified into something she carried daily.

At the shop, where she spends six days a week, the triggers are not abstract. A customer once came in with a bandaged arm and a visible IV port from an outpatient procedure, and Malia had to excuse herself to the back room. She keeps a small first-aid kit behind the counter as she always has, but she can no longer open it — the sight of the sterile packaging and the needle inside is enough to produce a rapid heartbeat and a tightening in her throat. She has rescheduled her own annual physical three times, unable to bring herself to enter a medical building. She asks her husband repeatedly, sometimes several times an evening, whether he thinks she seems healthy, whether he thinks she is okay. She cannot fully explain why his reassurances never quite settle the question for her.

She avoids films, music, and even family gatherings that might stir strong feeling — not just sadness, but anything that moves her, including joy. Her husband has noticed that she seems absent at celebrations, that she leaves the room when their grandchildren become loud with excitement. She has not been able to deliberately revisit the hospitalization in any structured way; when she tries, the memory resists her, remaining formless and inaccessible even as its emotional residue continues to surface unbidden.

What finally brought Malia to seek help was her son's upcoming wedding. She wants to be present for it — truly present — and she is afraid she will not be able to manage the emotions of the day. What she hopes for, she said quietly at the end of the intake, is simply to feel like herself again. What she fears most is that the person she was before those eleven days no longer exists.

Aleksander Nowak is a 34-year-old Polish-American firefighter who has been married for six years. He presents for an initial psychological evaluation following a humanitarian deployment to a conflict zone in Eastern Europe approximately fourteen months ago, during which he volunteered with an international relief organization for a period of three months. He describes the deployment as something he had pursued with genuine conviction, believing his emergency training would translate meaningfully into civilian rescue work. What he had not anticipated was the texture of sustained danger — the way threat did not arrive as a discrete event but as a constant atmospheric condition that eventually rewired something in him.

During his third week in the field, Aleksander's team was moving supplies through a corridor that had been declared temporarily safe. A vehicle approached from the opposite direction at speed, and in the seconds before it stopped, Aleksander could not determine whether it carried aid workers or combatants. Men emerged and moved toward the team quickly, and though the encounter resolved without violence — they were displaced civilians desperate for water — Aleksander describes those seconds of absolute uncertainty as the moment something broke open in him. It was not the only such moment, but it was the one he returns to most often. The men had come from nowhere, moving fast, and he had had no exit.

He returned home four months ago. His wife, Marta, noticed the changes before he named them. In their apartment, Aleksander began positioning himself near doorways during meals, angling his chair so his back was never fully to the room. When she asked about it, he said it was nothing. It was not nothing. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt less like a thought and more like a fact of physics, that any enclosed space without a clear way out was a space in which he could be trapped. He now scans exits automatically upon entering any building — the firehouse, the grocery store, their son's pediatric clinic — cataloguing them before he has fully registered where he is. Strangers who approach him in ordinary situations, a neighbor waving from across the parking lot, a man asking for directions, produce a spike of alarm that he recognizes as disproportionate but cannot override. He feels watched inside his own home, alert to sounds in a way that exhausts him but that he cannot simply decide to stop.

The consequences have accumulated quietly but concretely. Aleksander has stopped going to the gym, which had previously been a central part of his routine and his social life with colleagues. The physical arousal of exertion — the elevated heart rate, the heat, the breathlessness — became something he found intolerable in a way he struggled to articulate. It felt too close to something else. His absence from the gym has created distance from the two colleagues he trained with regularly, men who have not pushed him but who have noticed. At the firehouse, his captain has commented that he seems distracted during drills, and Aleksander is aware that his standing there, which had always been a source of pride, is quietly at risk.

Perhaps most troubling to Marta is something she cannot easily name: her husband seems to be refusing happiness. On their son's birthday last month, when the child laughed at something and reached for Aleksander's face, Aleksander felt something warm rise in him and then, almost immediately, pushed it away. He has come to feel that allowing himself to feel good, to soften, is a form of lowering his guard that he cannot afford. He does not know how to explain this to Marta without sounding, as he puts it, insane.

What finally brought him to seek help was a conversation with his captain, who quietly suggested that Aleksander speak to someone before his next fitness evaluation. He came reluctantly, framing it as a practical necessity. But in the first session, when asked what he was hoping for, he paused for a long time before saying he wanted to be able to sit in a room with his family and not be somewhere else entirely.

Parisa is a 26-year-old non-binary veterinarian of Iranian descent who presented for psychological assessment approximately four months after being mugged at knifepoint outside a convenience store near their apartment. It was a Tuesday evening in late autumn; Parisa had stopped to buy supplies on the way home from a long clinic shift. A man approached from behind, pressed something cold and sharp against their ribs, and demanded their phone and wallet. What Parisa remembers most viscerally is not the knife but the smell — cigarette smoke and something chemical, like cleaning fluid — and the sound of their own voice coming out thin and compliant, saying "okay, okay, take it, please." Within seconds the man was gone. Parisa stood on the pavement for a long moment, then walked home, and told themselves, as they unlocked the door, that it had not really been that serious. Nobody had been hurt. It was over.

That minimisation — the insistence that the event was not that bad — offered brief relief but quietly prevented Parisa from processing what had happened. Over the following weeks, they noticed that any time they tried to explain the mugging to their partner or a colleague, the thread of the account dissolved; they would lose the sequence, trail off, and change the subject. The memory had not been laid down as a coherent narrative but as fragments: the pressure against their ribs, the smell, the sound of their own compliance. Because the memory remained disorganised and unresolved, it was easily ambushed by the environment. At the veterinary clinic where Parisa works, the sharp smell of antiseptic solution — a routine and unavoidable feature of the job — could instantly collapse the distance between then and now, flooding them with the full sensory weight of that evening. In those moments, still in scrubs and mid-procedure, Parisa would feel their heart hammering and their eyes begin to sweep the room.

That reflexive scanning had become near-constant. Parisa now checked behind themselves when walking between the parking lot and the clinic entrance, and remained alert even inside their own home, sitting with their back to the wall and listening to sounds in the hallway. They had come to believe, with quiet but firm conviction, that the world was fundamentally unpredictable and threatening — that you simply could not know what was coming next, and that being caught unguarded once was proof that vigilance was the only rational response. This heightened threat monitoring, however, kept the nervous system in a state of perpetual readiness that made intrusive recall far more likely: a shadow in the peripheral vision, a stranger's footstep behind them on the pavement, and the memory would surge back unbidden, sometimes with the smell arriving before any visual image.

The appraisals that had settled around the event were bleak and generalising. Parisa had come to feel that the person who had once moved through the world with relative ease and warmth was simply gone — that they used to be happy, and now were not, and that this was a permanent condition rather than a symptom. Alongside this was a corrosive sense that other people could not be relied upon: no one had intervened that evening, and their attempts to explain what happened had been met with what felt like inadequate understanding. These beliefs fed directly into Parisa's avoidance of going out, which had narrowed their life considerably. They drove to work and drove home; they no longer walked anywhere after dark. Their partner had begun to notice, and the resulting conversations — gentle but persistent — had started to feel like another demand for compliance, another situation in which Parisa found themselves agreeing and accommodating in order to reduce tension rather than from genuine desire.

The magical thinking that the event had not really been serious remained a recurring retreat, but it carried a cost: each time Parisa minimised what had happened, the memory stayed unintegrated and the threat appraisals went unchallenged, leaving the whole system intact and tightening. The belief that the world was dangerous kept Parisa scanning; the scanning kept triggering memory fragments; the memory fragments reinforced the belief that danger was everywhere and that they were permanently changed by it.

What finally brought Parisa to seek help was a moment at the clinic when, smelling the antiseptic as a colleague cleaned an instrument tray, they froze completely in front of a client and could not speak for nearly a minute. They were afraid, they said quietly at intake, that they were losing their ability to do the one thing that had always felt like solid ground. What they most hoped for was to stop feeling like a stranger in their own life.

Vignette: Sasha, Age 26

Sasha grew up in a household where their parents often reminded them that hard work and vigilance were the prices of safety. They took those lessons seriously, earning a veterinary degree by twenty-four and building a quiet, purposeful life in a mid-sized city. Their partner, Dani, describes them as someone who used to move through the world with an easy confidence — the kind of person who would walk home from the clinic at dusk without a second thought, earbuds in, replaying the day's surgeries in their mind.

That changed fourteen months ago on a Tuesday evening in October. Sasha was two blocks from their apartment when two men approached from behind. One pressed something hard into the small of their back. The other stood close enough that Sasha could smell cigarette smoke on his jacket. They were told not to turn around, not to scream. Sasha handed over their bag — phone, wallet, keys — and stood frozen against a brick wall while footsteps receded. The whole encounter lasted perhaps ninety seconds. Sasha stood there for several minutes afterward, unable to move, convinced the men were still nearby, convinced the pressure against their spine meant they had been shot and simply hadn't felt it yet.

They hadn't been. But something in those ninety seconds rearranged the architecture of how Sasha experiences the world.

In the weeks that followed, Sasha returned to the veterinary clinic because the animals needed them and because routine felt like the only rope left to hold. But the work that had once felt grounding now carries its own weight. When a dog comes in after a trauma — hit by a car, attacked by another animal — and the creature lies still on the table, eyes wide and breathing shallow, Sasha recognizes something in that stillness that they cannot name aloud. They work carefully and competently, but afterward they sometimes sit in the supply room for ten or fifteen minutes before they can face the waiting room again.

Sleep is the most honest record of what Sasha carries. Most nights they wake between two and four in the morning, heart already pounding before consciousness fully arrives, the smell of cigarette smoke sometimes so vivid they check the room. Dani has learned not to touch Sasha without speaking first in those moments. Once, early on, Dani reached over in the dark and Sasha was across the room before either of them understood what had happened.

During the day, Sasha maps exits. In the clinic, in restaurants, in the grocery store — they know where every door is before they know anything else about a room. They stopped using earbuds outside. They have not walked home from work since October of last year, even though it is seven minutes and a route they once loved. When Dani suggests it, gently, Sasha agrees it is probably fine and then finds a reason to drive.

What troubles Sasha most, and what they speak about with a kind of bewildered frustration, is the gap between what they know and what they feel. They know, intellectually, that the odds of being robbed again on that same street are vanishingly small. They know the men are unlikely to ever find them. They know ninety seconds should not cost this much. And yet their body has not received any of this information. Their nervous system runs a continuous background calculation of threat, and no amount of reasoning seems to reach it.

Sasha describes their relationship with Dani as loving but strained. Dani is patient, but Sasha can see the worry that has taken up residence in Dani's face, and they hate being the cause of it. They have begun declining social invitations more often, preferring the apartment, preferring the known. They miss the person they were before October — not dramatically, not with self-pity, but with the quiet, persistent grief of someone who has misplaced something essential and cannot quite remember where they last set it down.

Rodrigo is a 54-year-old Latino man who has worked as a parole officer for nearly two decades, a career he chose because he believed in accountability, in systems that could correct themselves, and in the possibility of rehabilitation. He is married, the father of two adult children, and by most external measures a composed and authoritative presence. He presented for treatment with a PCL-5 score of 68, reporting that he could no longer trust his own body or his own mind, and that something had broken in him that he was not sure could be repaired.

Approximately fourteen months before seeking help, Rodrigo was beaten by two fellow officers during a confrontation that began when he intervened in what he believed was an excessive use of force against a parolee he was supervising. What followed was swift and methodical: he was taken to a stairwell, and in the silence of that enclosed space — no radio chatter, no voices, just the sound of the building settling — the beating began. He remembers the first blow, the cold of the concrete floor, and then fragments: a boot, a voice saying something low and flat, the feeling that time had become discontinuous. He was left there. No one came for a long time.

In the months that followed, Rodrigo found that the memory refused to form into a coherent whole. He described it as trying to hold water — pieces surfaced and then he pushed them back before they could fully resolve, because completing the picture felt intolerable. What he had managed to retrieve felt so extreme, so incongruent with his understanding of himself as someone inside the system rather than subject to it, that he sometimes doubted it had happened at all. And yet that very incompleteness kept the threat alive. Because the memory had no clean ending, no narrative closure, his mind remained convinced the danger was unresolved — that something was still coming. He could not locate the event safely in the past.

The appraisals that formed around the event became the psychological architecture of his daily life. He was certain he had been betrayed — not by strangers, but by colleagues he had worked alongside for years, men who understood exactly what they were doing and did it anyway. He was equally certain that nothing would be done: the internal investigation had been cursory, the findings inconclusive, and he had been quietly reassigned. What happened to him was deeply unfair, and the institution that was supposed to protect him had instead protected the men who hurt him. These convictions did not remain abstract. They fed directly back into the triggers themselves: when he witnessed someone in his caseload being disrespectful or defiant — a parolee cutting him off, raising their voice — the moral violation activated not just professional irritation but the full weight of his appraisal that authority cannot be trusted and that transgression goes unpunished. The boundary between then and now collapsed.

At work, the environment had become a landscape of threat signals. Unusual silence — an empty corridor, a room that went quiet when he entered — produced an immediate and visceral alarm, the same silence that had preceded the beating. He found himself scanning every room he entered, cataloguing exits, watching hands, reading faces for signs of what was about to happen. The startle response had become so pronounced that a door slamming two offices away could leave him gripping his desk. When stress accumulated across a workday, his heart would begin to race, and the racing itself became a trigger — his body's signal interpreted as confirmation that something dangerous was near, which in turn sharpened his vigilance, which surfaced more fragments of the memory, which deepened his conviction that the threat was ongoing and that no institution would intervene on his behalf.

His wife had noticed the change before he had named it. He had stopped talking about work. He had stopped sleeping through the night. He had become, in her words, someone who was always listening for something she couldn't hear.

What finally brought Rodrigo to seek help was a moment at work when he found himself standing in a stairwell — identical in layout to the one where the assault occurred — and was unable to move for several minutes. He told his intake clinician that he was not afraid of dying. What frightened him most was that the people who were supposed to be on his side never would be, and that he had begun to believe it had always been that way.

Kiet Nguyen is a twenty-two-year-old Vietnamese-American UX designer who presents with a PCL-5 score of 56 following a devastating earthquake that struck while he was visiting extended family in central Vietnam eighteen months ago. The quake hit without warning in the early morning, collapsing part of the house around him. He remembers the particular pressure of a ceiling beam across the back of his neck, the acrid taste of plaster dust filling his mouth, and the sound of his aunt calling his name from somewhere he could not locate in the dark. Several family members were injured; one did not survive. He was evacuated within hours, but the event left a mark on him that has not loosened its grip.

In the weeks that followed his return to the United States, Kiet noticed that certain experiences seemed to reach directly into that morning and pull it forward. A stiff neck after long hours at his workstation — entirely ordinary for someone who spends his days arranging wireframes and prototyping interfaces — would arrive as something else entirely: the pressure of the beam, the dust on his tongue, the sense that the walls were still moving. The somatic pain in his neck functions as one of the most reliable triggers he knows, and when it fires, the memory does not return as a coherent narrative so much as an atmosphere — taste without image, dread without scene, the full emotional weight of the event arriving before any picture forms. He has described sitting at his desk, feeling suddenly and inexplicably ill, the nausea and physical unwellness spreading through him, and finding himself back in that collapsed room without being able to say exactly how he got there. Hearing colleagues mention anything adjacent to the disaster — a news segment about flooding, a conversation about structural damage — operates the same way, the triggers pulling the memory forward with a force that feels disproportionate and humiliating.

What troubles Kiet as much as the intrusions themselves is what they seem to confirm about the world. Each time the memory surfaces — fragmentary, overwhelming, tasting of plaster — he finds it harder to hold onto any stable sense of his surroundings or the people in them. The memory carries a quality of unreality that has seeped outward: the event was so extreme, so far outside anything he had been prepared for, that he has come to feel that ordinary life is a kind of performance, and that people around him are similarly performing a safety they do not actually possess. He has grown convinced that people are not what they seem — that the colleagues who laugh easily at lunch, the friends who make weekend plans, are either unaware of how fragile everything is or are concealing it. This appraisal of others as unknowable and fundamentally unreliable has in turn narrowed his world considerably. He avoids team social events at the design agency where he works, declines invitations, and has stopped visiting the gym where he used to train, partly because the physical exertion reliably produces neck tension that he cannot trust not to trigger him. The avoidance has not gone unnoticed: his manager recently commented on his withdrawal from collaborative sessions, and a close friend from college stopped reaching out after several unanswered messages.

The sense that people cannot be trusted has itself become a source of new triggers. Moments of social friction — a misread message, a colleague's ambiguous expression — now carry a charge they did not before, confirming his belief that he does not belong among people who have not been through what he has. He has come to feel isolated and set apart in a way that feels permanent rather than circumstantial, and more recently he has begun to feel that he no longer belongs anywhere at all — not in the United States, where the disaster feels unreal to everyone around him, and not in Vietnam, which he associates entirely with what happened. This sense of belonging nowhere has made ordinary life feel like an extended waiting room, and the isolation itself keeps him alert for signs of threat, so that even benign physical sensations or passing references to disaster pull the memory forward again.

What finally brought Kiet to seek help was a presentation at work he could not complete — he had been storyboarding a user journey when a colleague mentioned an earthquake in the news, and he left the room and did not return. He is most afraid that nothing will feel real or safe again. What he hopes, cautiously, is that someone can help him understand why he cannot simply leave that morning behind.

# The Weight of Still Water

Kai is twenty-two years old, a UX designer at a small digital agency in the city, and by most outward appearances he is doing exactly what a young man his age should be doing — building a career, learning his craft, navigating his twenties. His colleagues know him as quiet and meticulous, someone who can spend hours refining the flow of a single interface until it feels effortless to the user. What they do not know is that he has not slept a full night in fourteen months.

In the spring of last year, Kai traveled back to his home province in the Philippines to visit his grandmother and extended family. He had grown up partly in that coastal town — a place of warm evenings, fishing boats, and the particular smell of salt and woodsmoke that he associated with childhood safety. He was there for three days when the typhoon made landfall. The storm surge came faster than anyone had anticipated. Kai remembers standing at the window watching the street turn into a river, and then the water was inside, and then it was at his waist, and then he was holding his grandmother's arm while she lost her footing and the current pulled her from his grip. She was recovered alive, found clinging to a neighbor's roof three streets away. He did not know this for nearly six hours.

Those six hours are where Kai lives now, even when he is sitting at his desk in an air-conditioned office in the city.

The intrusions arrive without warning or invitation. He will be reviewing a prototype — a simple onboarding screen, blue and white and completely ordinary — and the color will shift in his peripheral vision and suddenly he is back in that room, water rising, his grandmother's wrist sliding through his fingers. His heart rate spikes before his conscious mind has registered anything. He pushes back from his desk, excuses himself to the bathroom, and waits for the sensation to pass. It usually takes about ten minutes. He has become very good at finding reasons to step away.

At night, sleep is a negotiation he often loses. He keeps the television on, low volume, because silence feels like the moment just before the water came through the door. When he does sleep, he wakes from dreams that are not quite replays — sometimes the water is black, sometimes his grandmother does not come back — and he lies in the dark with his chest tight, running through what he knows to be true: she is alive, she is fine, he is in the city, he is safe. The reassurance helps, but only partially, and only for a while.

He has stopped going to the beach. This is not a small thing for someone who grew up swimming in the South China Sea. His friends invite him to weekend trips and he declines with easy excuses — a deadline, a freelance project, fatigue. He has become skilled at the architecture of avoidance, which perhaps makes sense for someone who spends his professional life designing the paths people take through spaces. He knows what it means to remove friction. He has removed every possible path that leads back toward water, toward flooding news coverage, toward the particular sound of heavy rain against glass.

What troubles him most, he says, is not the fear itself but the person the fear has made him. He describes himself before the typhoon as someone who was "open" — willing to travel, to try things, to be present with people he loved. Now he feels like he is watching his own life through a screen, always one step removed, always monitoring the edges of the frame for something that might go wrong. He worries that the person he was before the water came in is someone he cannot find his way back to, and he is not entirely sure he knows how to design a path toward that.

Rangi Taufa is a 71-year-old Tongan-American man who has been married for over forty years and works part-time as a cashier at a grocery store in a mid-sized Pacific Northwest city. He came to the clinic several months after the event that changed him, referred by his primary care physician who had grown concerned about his withdrawn affect and persistent sleep difficulties. He sat quietly in the intake session, hands folded in his lap, and spoke in careful, measured sentences — until he couldn't.

Approximately eight months ago, Rangi was present at a community gathering held in the fellowship hall of his church when a violent altercation broke out between two men near the entrance. One of the men produced a weapon. What followed lasted perhaps two minutes, though Rangi cannot account for the sequence with any confidence. A young mother who had been standing near the doorway was struck. Her infant, who had been in her arms, began to cry — a sound that cut through the noise of the hall in a way Rangi describes as impossible to unhear. He was close enough to see everything and far enough to be unable to intervene. By the time the situation was contained, the woman had sustained serious injuries. The men responsible were removed from the scene, but in the months that followed, no formal charges were pursued. The church leadership, where Rangi had worshipped for over twenty years, declined to discuss the matter publicly and made no formal acknowledgment to those who had witnessed it. Rangi was never contacted by anyone in an official capacity.

In the weeks that followed, something shifted in him that he struggled to name. He had come to feel, with a quiet but absolute certainty, that the institution he had trusted most had simply closed its doors on what happened — and on him. He did not speak of this readily, but it sat in him like a stone. He had also come to believe, though he found it difficult to articulate, that the people responsible had simply moved on while he remained anchored to a moment he could not fully reconstruct. When he tried to explain what had happened — to his wife, to his doctor, to the intake clinician — he would begin and then lose the thread entirely, sometimes mid-sentence, sometimes before he had even reached the moment of violence itself. He described the memory as a collection of fragments with gaps between them, like a photograph torn into pieces and reassembled with pieces missing. He could not tell a coherent story of the event even to himself, and this disturbed him in ways he did not fully understand.

At the grocery store where he works three shifts a week, Rangi stands behind his register near the main entrance. The automatic doors open and slam throughout his shift — a sound that, on certain days, sends a jolt through his body before he has had time to think. He has developed a habit of watching customers as they approach his lane, tracking their hands, their posture, the direction of their gaze, alert for something he cannot quite name but is certain he would recognize if it appeared. Shoppers with infants in carts present a particular difficulty; the sound of a crying baby — even a brief, ordinary cry — can stop him mid-transaction. He has twice needed to ask a colleague to cover his register, offering no explanation.

At home, Rangi describes feeling, much of the time, as though he is observing his own life from a distance. He participates in family dinners, accompanies his wife to appointments, tends his small garden — but reports feeling little of what he used to feel doing these things. He used the phrase "dead inside" without apparent distress, as though he had already made a kind of peace with it, or perhaps simply run out of language to protest it.

What finally brought him to seek help was his wife. She told him, gently but plainly, that she felt she had lost him. He did not disagree with her. What he hopes for, he said at the end of the intake session, is simply to understand what happened — to be able to hold the story of that night in a way that makes some kind of sense. What he fears is that he never will.

Fatima is a 45-year-old divorced Middle Eastern woman who works as an auditor for a mid-sized federal contracting firm in the Washington, D.C. area. She was referred for psychological evaluation following a period of escalating distress that had begun to compromise her functioning at work and left her, by her own account, "living inside four walls and still not feeling safe." Her trauma history centres on a period of combat exposure during a deployment-adjacent role she held in her late twenties, when she served as a civilian analyst embedded with a military unit operating in a conflict zone. On the day that would come to define the years that followed, her convoy was struck by an improvised explosive device. The blast was close enough that she was thrown from her seat, and in the immediate aftermath she found herself moving through smoke and debris, passing bodies and calling out names, uncertain who had survived and who had not. A particular detail she returns to involuntarily is the smell — a colleague's cologne, distinctive and expensive, present in the vehicle that morning and then present again, she believes, near one of the casualties. She cannot be certain. That uncertainty is part of what haunts her.

Fatima's memories of the event are fragmented in ways that distress her deeply. There are stretches she simply cannot account for — intervals between the blast and her eventual evacuation that exist in her recollection only as disconnected images: a door frame, a colour, a sound that wasn't language. She has come to believe that these gaps mean she is missing something critical, some piece of evidence that would either confirm or refute the conviction she carries most heavily — that she failed to protect the people in her care. The incomplete picture her memory offers does not feel neutral to her; it feels like an accusation, and the absence of a coherent narrative has allowed her worst interpretation to fill the space. This sense that the event happened because of the kind of person she is — not unlucky, but fundamentally insufficient — has calcified over the years into something she treats as established fact.

That appraisal of herself as someone who failed and who, at some level, deserved what followed has done considerable work in shaping how Fatima now moves through the world. She is certain that danger is not merely possible but imminent, and this certainty organises her daily life around a logic of containment and surveillance. She identifies escape routes before she will sit down in any room, including the conference rooms at her office where she conducts quarterly audits — a professional setting that has become a quiet theatre of threat management. She checks behind her when she walks between floors, and she has quietly mapped her workplace into zones of relative safety, rarely venturing into the open-plan areas near the building's large atrium windows. The sense of persistent threat, in turn, keeps her memory activated and primed: when she is hypervigilant, fragments surface more readily, and each surfacing fragment reinforces her belief that she has not yet fully understood what she did wrong.

The triggers that break through her defences are specific and visceral. An explosion or sharp bang — a car backfiring in the parking garage, a door slamming on the floor above — sends her immediately into a state of physical alarm that she finds humiliating, her body treating a mundane sound as evidence of incoming fire. Waking from a nightmare, she carries the residue of the dream into her morning in ways that make the workday feel like a continuation of the event rather than a departure from it. And the cologne — she encountered it on a male colleague last spring, and the olfactory ambush was so complete that she left the meeting early and did not return for the rest of the day. Each of these intrusions pulls fragmented memory to the surface, and each fragment she recovers seems to sharpen her self-blame rather than resolve it. To manage the triggers, she has retreated: she avoids open or exposed spaces, constantly scans her environment, and rehearses counterfactual narratives — what would have happened if she had made different choices, if she had been a different kind of person — as though thinking it through one more time might finally produce an answer that exonerates her. It does not. The rumination keeps the appraisals vivid and the threat sense elevated, which in turn makes the triggers more potent, and the cycle tightens.

What finally brought Fatima to seek help was a performance review in which her supervisor noted that she had been "difficult to reach" and had missed two client-facing meetings without explanation. She is afraid, she says quietly, that she is disappearing. What she hopes for, with some difficulty articulating it, is to one day walk into a room without first calculating how to leave it.

Rangi Taufa is a 71-year-old Tongan-American man who has been married for over forty years and works as a cashier at a large grocery store in a suburb of Salt Lake City. He presented for psychological assessment with a PCL-5 score of 57, describing a level of distress that had quietly accumulated over several years before finally becoming, in his own words, "too heavy to carry alone."

Approximately three years ago, Rangi witnessed a violent incident in his neighbourhood in which a young mother and her infant were attacked outside an apartment building. He was standing near the entrance when the assault began — the door swung open with force, the baby began screaming, and the violence unfolded in front of him before anyone could intervene. He called emergency services but felt paralysed, unable to act further. The perpetrator was known to the building's management and, in Rangi's view, had been reported and ignored on multiple prior occasions. No meaningful legal consequences followed. Rangi returned home that night and has not spoken about what he saw in any coherent way since.

What makes Rangi's situation clinically complex is the fractured nature of his memory of the event. He reports feeling as though he is only remembering parts of what happened, with large sections simply absent, and when he attempts to recount it — even to himself — he loses the thread entirely and cannot finish. This absence of a coherent narrative means that rather than processing the event as something contained in the past, Rangi experiences it as perpetually unresolved, and the fragmented quality of his memory keeps him in a state of chronic alertness. When a fragment does surface — the force of the door, the pitch of the infant's cry — it does not arrive as a bounded recollection but as a live signal, and in its wake the sounds and sensations that surrounded the original event become charged once more: a door banging in the store, a baby's wail from the next aisle, a sudden jolt of bodily discomfort all feel, in those moments, indistinguishable from the event itself. He cannot locate the event in time, and so his nervous system treats it as ongoing. When fragments surface, they tend to arrive not as story but as sensation — and those sensations have become tightly bound to specific features of the world around him.

The sound of a baby crying, a door opening or slamming, any sudden feeling of discomfort in his body — these are the threads that pull him back. At the grocery store where he works, these triggers are inescapable. Customers push through the automatic doors with a bang; parents wheel infants past his register; the ambient noise of the store is punctuated constantly by sounds that his nervous system has marked as warnings. Each trigger lands not merely as an unpleasant reminder but as a signal of imminent danger, sending him into a state of heightened alertness in which he scans nearby customers for signs of threat, braces against unexpected movement, and monitors everyone who approaches his lane. His colleagues have noticed that he seems tense and watchful, and one supervisor gently asked whether he was feeling well — a conversation Rangi deflected and has since avoided repeating.

The triggers do more than activate his threat system. They also pull forward the bitterest of his appraisals: that the people who should have protected that mother and child failed to do so, and that no one was ever held accountable. But the relationship runs in the other direction as well: the sheer persistence of the alarm — the way his body floods with danger at the sound of a door, day after day, year after year — has become its own argument. Feeling this afraid, this constantly, has quietly convinced Rangi that the fear must be warranted, that a world capable of producing such unrelenting dread is precisely the kind of world where harm is permitted to continue unchecked and where no one in authority can be trusted to stop it. Each time a door slams and his body floods with alarm, he is not only frightened — he is reminded of that institutional failure, and the anger and helplessness that come with it. He has come to feel, in a way he finds difficult to articulate, that the world is a place where harm is permitted to continue unchecked. This belief in turn feeds his vigilance: if institutions cannot be trusted to prevent violence, then he must watch for it himself. He monitors people closely, reads their movements, and stays on guard — not as a choice but as a compulsion that exhausts him.

The appraisals themselves seem to act as a barrier to memory processing. When Rangi tries to approach what he witnessed, the weight of feeling let down and the absence of any resolution make it feel intolerable to stay with the fragments long enough to form anything coherent. The story remains broken. And the broken story, cycling back, keeps the triggers sharp and the threat system primed.

What finally brought Rangi to seek help was his wife's observation that he had become unreachable — present in the house but absent in every way that mattered. He describes feeling dead inside. What he is most afraid of is that this is simply who he is now. What he is hoping, quietly, is that someone can help him find the rest of the story.

Linh is a 57-year-old Vietnamese American woman, married and the owner of a small convenience store in a mid-sized city. She was referred for psychological assessment following a conversation with her primary care physician, who noted that she had been avoiding routine blood tests for nearly three years and had become visibly distressed during a recent examination. Her PCL-5 score of 33 places her in the clinically significant range, and what follows is a portrait of how a single, devastating period in her life has quietly reorganised the architecture of her daily existence.

Approximately four years ago, Linh's youngest daughter, then nineteen, was admitted to hospital with a rapidly progressing infection that within forty-eight hours became life-threatening. Linh was present for much of it: the IV drips threading into her daughter's arms, the nurses drawing blood at intervals, the monitors, the smell of antiseptic, the particular quality of fluorescent light in a paediatric intensive care unit. Her daughter survived, but the weeks that followed the discharge were not relief so much as a delayed collapse. Linh found herself unable to account for what had happened in any language she trusted. She knew the sequence of events, but when she tried to reach for it deliberately, the memory seemed to dissolve — she could feel the weight of those days without being able to reconstruct them clearly, and sometimes the full emotional force of the crisis would arrive without any accompanying image, a grief with no picture attached. This fragmented quality of the memory meant that it never felt finished, never felt survivable in the way that a coherent story might.

The incompleteness of the memory fed directly into her interpretation of what had happened. Linh had come to believe, with a quiet but consuming certainty, that the hospital had not acted quickly enough in those first hours — that the people responsible for protecting her daughter had failed, and that nothing had been done to acknowledge this. She felt the injustice of it as a physical weight. And because the memory surfaced not as narrative but as sensation, the appraisals it generated were correspondingly raw: she had been there, she had not insisted loudly enough, she had failed to protect her own child. These beliefs, once formed, made the triggers she encountered all the more unbearable. When a customer at the store paid for bandages and she caught sight of blood on their hand, or when a pharmaceutical supplier delivered a box containing syringes, the sight alone was enough to pull her back into the ward — not into a clear memory, but into the emotional core of it, the helplessness and the terror.

The hypervigilance that developed in the months after her daughter's discharge further tightened this pattern. Linh found she could not relax even in the back room of her own shop, scanning customers and the street outside as though danger were always imminent. This constant state of alert made her body exquisitely sensitive to any reminder, so that a routine physical examination at her GP became almost unbearable, her heart rate spiking the moment the doctor reached for the blood pressure cuff. The physical reactivity reinforced her sense that something was still fundamentally wrong — which in turn reactivated the appraisals of institutional failure and personal culpability, and sharpened her attention to anything that might signal a new threat.

To manage this, Linh developed a set of strategies that brought short-term relief but gradually narrowed her world. She began asking her husband repeatedly whether she seemed well, whether he thought she was coping — reassurance that satisfied her for minutes before the doubt returned. She tried actively to suppress the memory, to push it away whenever it approached, though this effort paradoxically left her more sensitised to the triggers that might summon it. She began avoiding not only medical settings but anything that might produce strong feeling of any kind, withdrawing from family celebrations and the small pleasures of her shop. This emotional blunting meant she was less equipped to process what had happened, which kept the appraisals of injustice and failure alive and unresolved, and left her body in a state of readiness that no amount of scanning ever resolved.

What finally brought her to seek help was a missed appointment for a mammogram — the third consecutive year she had cancelled it. Her husband, who had watched the slow contraction of her life with increasing worry, sat with her one evening and said, quietly, that he was frightened for her. Linh told the clinician she did not expect to feel better. What she hoped for, she said, was to be able to take care of herself without it feeling like walking back into the ward.

# The Weight of the Plaza

Roberto is a seventy-year-old retired dentist who still keeps the hours of a working man. He wakes at six, dresses carefully, and drives to his small office three mornings a week, though he sees only a handful of patients now — mostly old neighbors who have been coming to him for decades. The routine, he says, is the only thing that keeps the days from blurring together.

Eighteen months ago, Roberto was sitting at an outdoor café in the central plaza of the city where he had practiced for forty years, waiting for his wife, Marisol, to finish shopping at the market across the street. He was reading the newspaper and drinking his second coffee of the morning when the car bomb detonated. The blast threw him from his chair. He remembers the sound — not a bang, but a pressure, something that seemed to push through his chest and rearrange everything inside him. When he opened his eyes, the plaza was unrecognizable. The café's glass facade was gone. There was smoke and dust and a stillness that lasted only a second before the screaming began. Marisol had been standing near the market entrance. She did not survive.

Roberto was treated for a perforated eardrum and lacerations to his face and arms. He was discharged from the hospital after two days. The funeral arrangements fell to him, and he moved through them with a mechanical efficiency that he now recognizes as a kind of shock. His children flew in from abroad. People brought food. Then, gradually, everyone went home, and Roberto was left alone in the house he and Marisol had shared for forty-three years.

He does not sleep well. Most nights he lies awake until two or three in the morning, his mind replaying the sequence of events in the plaza with a precision that feels involuntary, almost punishing — the newspaper folded on the table, the taste of the coffee, the particular quality of the morning light before everything changed. When he does sleep, he wakes abruptly, heart pounding, certain he has heard an explosion. He checks the windows. He checks the locks.

During the day, Roberto avoids the city center entirely. He has not returned to the plaza. He takes longer routes to his office, routes that bypass any street he associates with that morning. Loud noises — a car backfiring, a door slamming in the hallway — cause him to flinch and freeze in a way that embarrasses him. He is a composed man, a professional, and he finds his own reactions bewildering and, at times, humiliating.

What troubles him most, he says quietly, is the guilt. He had been the one to suggest the café. He had chosen the table outside because the weather was fine. He turns this over and over, the way a tongue finds a sore tooth. His daughter has told him it was not his fault. He nods when she says this. He does not believe it.

Roberto finds little pleasure in things that once sustained him. He used to play chess on Sunday afternoons with a group of retired colleagues. He stopped going after the third or fourth time he found himself unable to follow the game, his attention pulled elsewhere, to somewhere he could not name but could not leave. He still goes to Mass, though he sits near the exit and leaves before the final blessing. He is not sure anymore what he is praying for.

He describes himself as tired in a way that sleep does not fix. He says the world feels thinner now, like a photograph of itself. He misses Marisol with a grief that is inseparable from everything else he carries — the blast, the guilt, the sleepless nights — all of it fused into a single, heavy thing he carries with him into his quiet office each morning, where he puts on his white coat and asks his patients to open wide.

Vignette: Mae

Mae is a 57-year-old married woman of Thai descent who has run a small fabric and sewing notions shop in the same neighborhood for nearly twenty years. She is soft-spoken and precise in the way she describes things — the kind of person who folds cloth along exactly the right grain before she cuts it. That same precision, she says, is what makes it so hard when her mind refuses to stay where she puts it.

Eight years ago, Mae's youngest son, Decha, then fourteen, collapsed at school during a physical education class. What followed was three weeks in a pediatric intensive care unit, a diagnosis of viral myocarditis, two episodes where physicians told Mae and her husband that Decha might not survive the night, and an emergency transfer to a larger hospital two hours from their home.
