Mae slept in waiting rooms. She watched nurses move quickly and quietly around her son's bed in ways that told her more than any doctor's words. She remembers the particular sound of the cardiac monitor — a steady, ordinary beep that she learned to listen to with her whole body, terrified of any change. Decha survived. He is now a healthy young man in university. Mae knows this. She reminds herself of it often. It does not always help.

In the years since, Mae has rebuilt most of the surface of her life. The shop opens at nine. She orders inventory, advises customers on thread weight and interfacing, teaches a small alterations class on Thursday evenings. Her husband notices that she seems fine. She mostly is, in the way that a person can be fine while carrying something heavy in both hands.

What Mae does not tell many people is that she still cannot hear a certain kind of alarm — a medical alert tone, the beep of a truck reversing, even the timer on her shop's back-room microwave — without her chest tightening and her hands going cold. She has replaced the microwave timer with a silent visual model. She does not fully understand why she did this until she tries to explain it here.

She avoids the hospital where Decha was first admitted. This means she has not visited a neighbor who was recently treated there, something that troubles her conscience. She tells herself she is busy with the shop. She knows that is not the whole truth.

Sleep is where the past finds her most reliably. She wakes between two and four in the morning, sometimes from a dream in which she is standing outside a glass door she cannot open, watching a monitor she cannot read. Other times she simply wakes, already frightened, without knowing why. She lies still so as not to disturb her husband, running through a mental inventory of everyone she loves, checking that they are accounted for. She has become, she says with a small, self-aware laugh, "a woman who needs to know where everyone is."

When Decha calls home less frequently during exam periods, Mae finds herself constructing quiet catastrophes. She will send a casual message and wait for the reply with a vigilance she recognizes as disproportionate but cannot quite release. She describes this as feeling like standing at the edge of something, always. She is not depressed, she is careful to say. She loves her life. She loves her shop, her husband, her son. It is more that the world has shown her, once, in vivid and undeniable detail, exactly how quickly everything can change, and she has not entirely found her way back from that knowledge.

She came to therapy, she explains, because Decha recently had a routine cardiac follow-up appointment, and for the two weeks beforehand Mae could not eat a full meal. She sat behind the shop counter and cut fabric and smiled at customers and felt, the entire time, as though she were still in that waiting room — still listening, still watching the door.

Rodrigo Mendes is a 54-year-old married Latino man who has worked as a parole officer for nearly two decades, a career built on the conviction that systems of accountability, when functioning properly, can redirect lives. He presents now with a PCL-5 score of 68, having resisted seeking help for what he describes, with visible discomfort, as something that should not have happened to him — not in the way it did, not by the hands it came from.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Rodrigo was returning home after a late shift, still in civilian clothes, when he was stopped by two officers in a neighborhood adjacent to his jurisdiction. What began as a routine stop escalated with a speed he still cannot fully account for. He was ordered to the ground, and when he moved to identify himself as law enforcement, one of the officers struck him repeatedly — across the back, then across the side of his head — before he could finish the sentence. He remembers the cold of the pavement against his cheek, the sound of his own breathing loud in his ears, and then a period he cannot reconstruct with any confidence. What he can recall arrives in fragments: a voice on a radio, the pressure of a knee, a silence that fell over the scene that felt, he says, like the world had stopped deciding what would happen to him. He was eventually released without charge. No report was filed. No officer faced review.

In the weeks that followed, Rodrigo found himself unable to sit comfortably in the silences that are unavoidable in his work — the pause before a parolee answers a question, the quiet of an empty hallway between interviews. Each of those silences carries for him now the quality of that moment on the pavement, when nothing was happening yet and everything was about to. He has come to feel, with a certainty he cannot reason his way out of, that unusual quiet signals imminent danger, and he finds himself scanning the room constantly during client meetings — checking exits, watching hands, reading posture in ways that exceed professional habit. He startles badly when doors open behind him, something his colleagues have noticed and quietly remarked upon.

His own body has become unreliable in a different way. When his heart rate rises — from climbing stairs between floors at the office, from a difficult phone call, from nothing he can identify — he is pulled immediately toward the physical memory of that night, the adrenaline and the helplessness arriving together. He does not complete the thought when it begins. He has developed a practiced interruption, a way of pushing the memory back before it can fully surface, which means he has never been able to reconstruct a coherent account of the event even for himself. The story feels, he says, like something that happened to someone else — too extreme, too wrong to have been his actual life — and yet the gaps in it trouble him precisely because he knows something is missing and cannot retrieve it.

What sits most heavily on Rodrigo is not the physical memory but the meaning he has drawn from it. He had trusted, implicitly and professionally, in the integrity of law enforcement accountability. He had built his working life on that trust. What happened to him shattered that framework entirely, and the absence of any institutional response — no acknowledgment, no consequence, no correction — has left him with a sense of injustice that has no outlet. He was betrayed, he believes, not only by the officers who harmed him but by every structure that was supposed to prevent exactly this. That belief has altered how he sits across from his own clients — men and women navigating a system he once defended without reservation — in ways he finds deeply disorienting.

His wife noticed the change in him long before he named it, and it was her quiet insistence, over many months, that finally brought him to this office. What Rodrigo fears most is that telling the story fully — to the extent he even can — will confirm that nothing about it will ever be made right. What he hopes for, more tentatively, is that he might find a way to carry it without it continuing to occupy every silence in the room.

# The Weight of the Badge

Marco is a 54-year-old Colombian-American man who has spent the better part of three decades working as a parole officer in a mid-sized city in the American Southwest. He is broad-shouldered and deliberate in the way he speaks, a man who chose his career because he believed in second chances — a belief that now sits uneasily inside him, like something he swallowed that won't quite go down.

Four years ago, Marco was driving home from a late shift when he was pulled over in a neighborhood two miles from his house. He had done nothing wrong. He was in civilian clothes, his badge locked in the glove compartment. Before he could reach for it, two officers had him on the pavement, a knee on his neck, gravel pressing into his cheek. He remembers the cold of the asphalt, the smell of exhaust, the sound of his own voice — calm at first, then desperate — telling them he was law enforcement, telling them his name. He remembers thinking, with absolute clarity, that he was going to die on that street. The incident lasted eleven minutes. It felt like a lifetime compressed into something he can no longer fully unfold.

He drove himself home afterward, sat in the driveway for an hour, and said nothing to his wife, Esperanza, when he came through the door. He told her he was tired. That was true. He has been tired ever since.

In the weeks that followed, Marco found himself unable to sleep past three in the morning. He would lie rigid beside Esperanza, listening to the house settle, convinced something was wrong, though he could never say exactly what. When he did sleep, he woke from dreams that left him drenched and disoriented — dreams in which the pavement never ends, in which no one comes. He stopped taking the highway to work, rerouting through surface streets to avoid passing the intersection where it happened. He still does this, four years later, adding twenty minutes to every commute without ever consciously deciding to.

At work, Marco moves through his caseload with a kind of mechanical efficiency that his supervisor mistakes for professionalism. He supervises men and women who have been released from prison, many of them people of color, and he is good at his job — or he used to feel that way. Now, when he sits across from a young man who has been roughed up by police, Marco feels something shift behind his sternum, a recognition he doesn't know what to do with. He sometimes ends these meetings early. He tells himself he has paperwork.

He has stopped attending the monthly inter-agency meetings where parole officers sit alongside law enforcement. He submitted a medical excuse the first time. After that, no one asked.

Esperanza knows something is wrong. She has known since the night he came home silent and sat in the driveway. She has tried to reach him — gently at first, then more directly — and he responds by reassuring her, by changing the subject, by becoming very busy with small tasks around the house. He loves her and cannot explain to her what happened to him without also explaining what it means: that the institution he has given his life to nearly took his. He isn't ready for her to see how much that has unmade him.

He describes himself, in his more honest moments, as a man who used to believe in systems. He still goes to work. He still files his reports. He still stops at the same bakery on Thursday mornings and orders the same coffee. But somewhere beneath all of that routine, Marco is still lying on cold pavement, still waiting for someone to believe him, still listening for footsteps that may or may not be walking away.

Nadia Khalil is a 26-year-old non-binary veterinarian of Lebanese descent who presented for psychological assessment approximately four months after being mugged at knifepoint on a Tuesday evening in the parking structure adjacent to the animal hospital where they work. Nadia had stayed late to monitor a post-operative patient and was walking to their car, hands full with a tote bag and a travel mug, when a man stepped from between two parked vehicles and pressed a blade against their ribs. He took their phone, their wallet, and the tote bag. The whole encounter lasted perhaps ninety seconds. What Nadia remembers most viscerally is the smell — motor oil and something sweetly chemical, like cheap cologne or solvent — and the sound of their own voice saying, without any prior decision, "Okay, okay, take it, please, take it," accommodating every demand with a kind of desperate, automatic softness. They were released unharmed. They drove home shaking. They did not call the police that night.

In the weeks that followed, Nadia continued to report to work, because the animals needed them and because stopping felt like admitting something they were not ready to admit. But the parking structure had become a gauntlet. They began arriving before dawn when the structure was better lit and leaving only with colleagues, scanning every concrete pillar and parked car for a silhouette that did not belong. Inside the hospital itself, when a large or agitated client stepped too close, Nadia felt their voice go soft and accommodating in the same automatic way it had in the structure, agreeing to things they did not mean, apologising for things that were not their fault. They recognised what was happening and felt ashamed of it, but the compliance arrived before the recognition, like a reflex.

At home, the vigilance did not switch off. Nadia's partner, Reem, noticed them checking the locks multiple times before bed, pausing at the sound of footsteps in the hallway outside their apartment, turning to look behind them when they walked from the kitchen to the bedroom. Nadia had come to believe, with a quiet but firm certainty, that safety was simply not guaranteed anywhere — not in a well-lit apartment, not with someone who loved them nearby. They could not rely on that love as a buffer. When Reem offered reassurance, Nadia heard it as something kind but structurally useless, the way a weather forecast is useless once it is already raining.

The intrusions arrived without schedule. A client's cologne in the exam room could return Nadia to the parking structure completely — not as a recollection but as a re-immersion, the smell of motor oil suddenly present, the pressure at their ribs suddenly real. When they tried to describe the mugging to Reem or to their supervisor — who had gently asked whether Nadia wanted to file an incident report — they found the account dissolving mid-sentence, the thread of it dropping somewhere they could not locate, leaving them standing in silence with their mouth open. After the second attempt, they stopped trying to explain.

What accumulated over months was a progressive narrowing. Nadia began declining evening social engagements, then weekend ones, then anything that required walking to a car alone or navigating unfamiliar streets. Reem had been patient, but the relationship had grown careful and slightly formal in the way relationships do when one person is managing something the other cannot fully reach. Professionally, Nadia's supervisor had begun scheduling them exclusively for daytime shifts, an accommodation Nadia had accepted with relief and then felt diminished by. They had trained for years to be capable. They had come to believe that person — the capable, curious, genuinely happy person who had chosen this work — was simply gone.

What finally brought Nadia to seek help was a morning when they sat in their car in the hospital parking structure for twenty-two minutes, unable to open the door. They told themselves, as they had many times before, that the mugging had not been that serious, that other people experienced far worse. The thought did not move them. They called the hospital to say they would be late, and then they called a therapist. What they most hope for, they said at intake, is to stop feeling like a stranger in their own life. What they most fear is that the person they were before that Tuesday evening is not recoverable.

# The Weight of Numbers

Fatima is a 45-year-old auditor who spent three years embedded with a humanitarian accounting team in a conflict zone, tracking financial flows through active war zones in the Middle East. She was meticulous, precise, and proud of her work — the kind of person who believed that accountability and transparency could, in some small way, reduce suffering. That belief ended on a Tuesday morning seven years ago when a convoy she was traveling in was ambushed on a road outside a provincial city. Two colleagues were killed in the vehicle directly ahead of hers. Fatima survived by lying beneath the body of a wounded colleague for nearly two hours, pressing her hands against his side wound while gunfire continued around them. He lived. She has never fully forgiven herself for the relief she felt when she finally heard friendly forces arrive.

She returned home to her family in Toronto within weeks, telling almost no one what had happened. Her marriage, already strained by her long absences, collapsed within a year. Her ex-husband described her as "gone" even when she was in the room. She did not disagree with him.

Fatima now works for a mid-sized accounting firm, auditing corporate financial statements from a quiet office where nothing, on the surface, should be dangerous. And yet danger finds her constantly, in forms that make no rational sense to her. The sound of a staple gun across the office floor sends her out of her chair. A car backfiring in the parking garage below her building means she cannot re-enter the elevator for the rest of the afternoon. She takes the stairs. She has learned the location of every exit in every building she enters, and she sits with her back to the wall in every meeting room, a habit her colleagues have quietly stopped remarking on.

Sleep is a negotiation she mostly loses. She falls asleep without difficulty — exhaustion sees to that — but she wakes between two and four in the morning with her heart hammering and the specific smell of that road in her nose, dust and diesel and something she cannot name and will not try to. She does not always remember the dream, but her body remembers everything. She showers at three in the morning more nights than not.

Her work, paradoxically, is where she functions best and worst simultaneously. The precision of auditing suits her hypervigilance — she catches discrepancies that junior staff miss entirely, and her supervisors regard her as exceptional. But she cannot delegate. She reviews everything herself because she cannot tolerate the possibility that something will be missed, that a small error will compound into catastrophe. She works sixty-hour weeks and calls it professionalism. Some days she recognizes it for what it actually is: the only way she knows how to feel in control.

She has largely withdrawn from her social world. She declined her sister's wedding invitation last year because the venue was in a hotel with a single entrance and no clear sightlines. She told her sister she was traveling for work. She was, in fact, at home, sitting in the dark in her kitchen, aware of exactly how irrational she was being and completely unable to stop. The shame of that evening sits in her chest like a stone she cannot put down.

She does not speak about the convoy. She has never spoken about the convoy, not to her ex-husband, not to her sister, not to her closest friend, who knows only that Fatima "had a hard time overseas." When the subject of the war in her home region appears on the news, she turns the television off immediately and goes to do something with her hands — washing dishes, reorganizing files, anything that requires counting. Numbers, she has discovered, are one of the few things that reliably bring her back to the present. She counts her steps. She counts her breaths. She counts the lines on a spreadsheet and feels, briefly, like someone who is still entirely here.

Vignette: Elena, Age 47

Elena has spent the better part of two decades working with vulnerable women in her community — survivors of domestic violence, trafficking, and poverty. She knows how to sit with other people's pain. What she has never quite learned is how to sit with her own.

Three years ago, Elena was sexually assaulted by a colleague — a man she had known for years, someone who shared her office, her mission, her faith. She had stayed late one evening to finish grant paperwork, and he had stayed too. She does not talk about what happened in detail. What she will say is that she drove home afterward, washed her clothes, and went to bed beside her husband without saying a word. She told herself she would deal with it later. Later has not come.

In the weeks after the assault, Elena threw herself into her work with an intensity that alarmed her supervisor. She was at the office before anyone else arrived and left after everyone had gone. She told herself she was needed. The women she served were in real danger — what had happened to her, she reasoned, was not something she had the right to fall apart over. She had seen worse. She had held the hands of women who had survived worse.

But her body refused to cooperate with this logic. She began having nightmares so vivid and physical that she would wake up choking, convinced someone was in the room. Her husband, Rodrigo, would reach for her in the dark and she would recoil from his touch before she was fully awake, then spend the rest of the night rigid with shame. Their marriage, once easy and affectionate, has become a careful, quiet distance that neither of them fully names.

At work, Elena can no longer attend the support groups she used to facilitate for assault survivors. She has handed those off to a younger colleague, citing administrative responsibilities. The truth is that sitting in that circle — listening to women describe what was done to them — sends her into a state she can only describe as disappearing. Her vision narrows. Her chest locks. She has learned to excuse herself before it becomes visible.

She is hypervigilant in ways that exhaust her. She parks in a different spot every day. She checks the office locks three times before leaving. When a male colleague lingers in a doorway, her body floods with adrenaline and she has to remind herself, slowly and deliberately, where she is. The man who assaulted her no longer works at the organization — he resigned quietly, months later, for reasons officially unrelated — but his absence has not made the building feel safe.

Elena has not told Rodrigo what happened. She has constructed a version of herself that functions, that makes dinner, that asks about his day. She is a skilled listener by profession, and she has turned that skill inward in the worst possible way — monitoring herself constantly for signs that she is becoming someone her family cannot recognize. She worries she is already there.

What brings her in now, three years later, is not a crisis but an accumulation. Last month, a young woman came into the ministry office and described her assault in language so precise and familiar that Elena had to leave the room. She sat in the bathroom for twenty minutes, shaking, before she could return. That evening, she looked up a therapist's number. She waited two weeks to call. When she finally did, she told the receptionist she was calling on behalf of a client.

She corrects herself at the first session, quietly, without elaborating. She is a woman who has spent her life advocating for others to seek help. She is still learning, at forty-seven, that the invitation was always meant for her too.

Kiet Bùi is a twenty-two-year-old Vietnamese-American UX designer who presented for an initial psychological evaluation approximately eight months after surviving a catastrophic tornado that tore through the rural Oklahoma town where he had been visiting his aunt's family over a long weekend. He had no prior history of trauma or mental health treatment, and at the time of the disaster he described himself as someone who moved through the world with relative ease — sociable, curious, absorbed in his work.

The tornado struck without adequate warning on a Saturday afternoon in early spring. Kiet had been sitting at his aunt's kitchen table eating a bowl of bún bò Huế when the sky outside the window turned a colour he later struggled to name — not green exactly, but wrong in a way that registered in his chest before his mind caught up. Within seconds the structure around him began to come apart. He was thrown from his chair and pinned beneath collapsed cabinetry for what he estimates was nearly forty minutes before emergency responders reached him. During that time he could not move his neck, could feel something warm and wet along his collarbone, and was certain, with a clarity that still disturbs him, that he was going to die alone in a stranger's kitchen. The smell of the spilled soup — star anise, lemongrass, a faint char from the gas line — was everywhere. His aunt was found in another part of the house, badly injured but alive. Two neighbours were not.

In the weeks that followed, Kiet returned to his apartment in Austin and attempted to resume his work as a UX designer at a mid-sized software firm. The physical injury to his neck had been treated, but a residual stiffness remained, and he noticed that whenever the tension in his neck flared — during long hours hunched over wireframes and prototype mockups — something would shift inside him that he could not name or contain. He would not necessarily see anything, would not replay the kitchen or the collapsed ceiling, but the full weight of that afternoon would arrive in him without an image attached to it, like a tide coming in through a door he couldn't locate. On other occasions the memory returned with a sensory precision that bewildered him: he would be sitting at his standing desk reviewing user-flow diagrams and suddenly taste star anise on the back of his tongue, sharp and unmistakable, as though the bowl were in front of him again. He found himself checking the weather application on his phone compulsively whenever he felt physically unwell — a mild headache, a wave of nausea — interpreting bodily discomfort as a signal that something catastrophic was imminent. Any news coverage of tornadoes, storm systems, or disaster relief efforts sent him immediately out of the room.

What unsettled Kiet most was not the physical intrusions but a quieter, more corrosive shift in how the world appeared to him. He had come to believe that people were fundamentally unknowable — that the warmth colleagues showed him at the office, the friendliness of his roommate, even his family's concern, concealed something unreliable beneath it. He was not sure what he expected people to reveal; he only knew that he no longer trusted the surface of things. He felt set apart from everyone around him, as though he were observing his own life through the glass of a user-testing booth — present but separated, watching behaviours he could no longer participate in naturally. The design work that had once felt collaborative and energising now required a performance of engagement he found exhausting. He stopped attending team stand-ups in person, citing audio quality, and began working almost exclusively through asynchronous messages. He had not seen friends socially in four months. What frightened him most was not any single symptom but the growing sense that there was no place — not Austin, not his family's home in San Jose, not anywhere — where he felt he still belonged. The memory of the tornado itself sometimes struck him as impossible, so extreme in its rupture of ordinary life that part of him could not fully accept that it had happened to him at all.

He sought help after his manager gently raised concerns about his withdrawal from the team, and after he found himself unable to finish a bowl of pho his roommate had made — leaving the table without explanation, unable to account for his own reaction. He came to the intake session hoping, in his words, to feel like he was part of things again.

Fatima Haddad is a 45-year-old divorced Iraqi-American woman who works as a senior auditor for a federal contracting firm in the Washington, D.C. area. She presents for her first formal psychological evaluation following more than two years of escalating distress that she has, until recently, managed largely in silence.

Fatima was born in Baghdad and immigrated to the United States in her early twenties. After completing her accounting degree, she built a stable professional life, raised two children with her then-husband, and eventually obtained a security clearance that allowed her to take on audit work for defense contractors. It was through this work, in 2021, that she was embedded with a civilian oversight team near a forward operating base in Afghanistan during the final weeks of the U.S. withdrawal. She was not a soldier, and she had not expected to be in danger. On the afternoon that changed everything, a vehicle-borne explosive detonated approximately forty meters from the administrative building where she and several colleagues were reviewing procurement documents. The blast collapsed part of the structure. Fatima survived with minor physical injuries, but two of her colleagues did not. In the immediate aftermath, she moved through the rubble, calling names, trying to locate people she had been sitting beside minutes earlier. She has never been able to fully account for what happened in those minutes. There are stretches of time from that afternoon she simply cannot retrieve — not suppressed in any way she can identify, just absent, as though the recording stopped. What she does retain comes in disconnected pieces: the particular quality of the light before the blast, the smell of a colleague's cologne — a warm, cedar-heavy scent he wore every day — and then noise, pressure, and fragments that do not assemble into a coherent sequence. She has come to feel that she is only in possession of parts of the story, that something essential is missing from her own memory of the worst day of her life.

In the months following her return to the United States, Fatima's symptoms developed gradually and then, it seemed to her, all at once. The nightmares began within weeks — vivid, disorienting, and difficult to shake. Waking from them did not bring relief so much as a suspended state of alarm that could last hours. On those mornings she would arrive at her office already exhausted, already watchful. Her work as an auditor requires her to move through large open office floors, federal buildings with wide atria, and occasionally outdoor government campuses. These environments had become intolerable to her in ways she found difficult to explain to colleagues. She began arriving early to map exits before others filled the space, identifying which stairwells were unlocked and which conference rooms offered a clear sightline to the door. She stopped accepting assignments that required working in exposed outdoor areas, citing scheduling conflicts, and her supervisor had begun to notice the pattern. A formal performance conversation last spring was what finally prompted her to seek help, though she has not disclosed the reason for her difficulties.

In public, Fatima moves through the world with a vigilance that is exhausting and that she cannot suspend. She frequently turns to check whether someone is following her in parking garages and corridors. Loud sounds — a car backfiring, a door slamming in an adjacent office — produce a physical response she describes with shame and bewilderment, as though her body has made a decision without consulting her. She had come to believe that this reactivity was evidence of something fundamentally wrong with her character, that a more capable or more resilient person would have recovered by now. Worse, she was certain that she had failed the colleagues who did not survive — that she had been in a position to do something and had not, though what that something might have been she cannot say. She has spent considerable time imagining the version of events in which she had pushed for the team to work from a different location that day, a line of thinking that offers no resolution and from which she cannot easily withdraw.

What brought Fatima to the intake appointment was not only the professional consequences but a quiet, frightening recognition: the world had contracted around her. She feels genuinely safe in almost no place outside her own apartment, and even there, the nightmares follow her. What she fears most in treatment is being asked to remember what she cannot. What she hopes for, stated plainly in her intake paperwork, is to be able to do her job again without feeling like she is waiting for something terrible to happen.

Amara is a 42-year-old Eritrean-born woman who came to the United States approximately six years ago following a period of detention and torture by state security forces in her home country. She works the early shift at a packaging factory in a mid-sized Midwestern city, is divorced, and lives alone in a small apartment. She presented for psychological services after what she described as "finally running out of ways to keep going."

The events that brought Amara to this point occurred over several weeks of captivity during which she was subjected to systematic physical torture. She was held in a facility where guards announced their arrival with the sound of a heavy metal door being dragged open — a grinding, scraping noise that preceded every session. The air in the cell was thick with a particular smell she has never been able to name precisely, something chemical and damp. It was the dry season, and the heat was relentless, the kind that pressed down without relief. One of her primary interrogators shared a name with her former brother-in-law, a name she had once associated only with family gatherings. By the time she was released and eventually resettled, the architecture of her daily life had been quietly restructured around the memory of those weeks, though she did not yet understand that this was what was happening.

In the factory, Amara operates a sealing machine at the end of a conveyor line. The work requires sustained attention, which she welcomed at first — keeping her mind occupied felt like survival. She has developed an elaborate internal practice of narrating tasks to herself, counting repetitions, rehearsing shopping lists, anything to prevent her thoughts from going quiet enough for the memory to surface. But the factory presents its own difficulties. When a colleague whose name is the same as that interrogator calls out across the floor, Amara's body responds before she has registered the sound consciously — her chest tightens, her hands freeze above the machine. She has asked her shift supervisor to change her station twice without explaining why. On particularly hot summer days, when the factory floor becomes stifling and the air sits heavy and still in a way that resembles the dry season of her captivity, she has left her post mid-shift, telling no one. This has resulted in two formal warnings, and she is now at risk of losing her position.

At home, Amara keeps the television on through the night and sleeps with a chair wedged under the front door handle. She listens constantly for sounds that might mean someone is entering — a creak on the stairs, a door in another apartment. When ordinary sounds occur, a dropped pan in the hallway or a car backfiring on the street below, she startles violently, her heart already racing before any thought has formed. She had come to believe, with a quiet certainty she rarely articulated, that her body could no longer be trusted to distinguish safety from danger, that it had been rewired into something she did not recognise. She wore certain clothes in the facility, and she has not worn anything resembling them since — particular colours, particular textures. She applies heavy makeup daily, a practice that began as a way of covering bruising in the months after her release and has since become something she cannot leave the apartment without. She cannot fully explain it except to say that without it she feels exposed in a way that frightens her.

What troubles Amara perhaps most deeply is the quality of the memory itself. When she thinks about what happened, it does not feel like something that happened to her. It feels borrowed, belonging to a woman she observes from a distance, someone extreme and foreign. She has said in session that the memory is so severe she sometimes cannot believe it is real — and yet when she catches a particular smell, chemical and damp, it arrives with a physical immediacy that collapses that distance entirely. She had come to believe that she was no longer the person she was before — the woman who had worked, raised a child, managed a household — and that this incapacity was permanent. What finally brought her to seek help was her daughter, now living with Amara's sister in another state, asking over the phone why her mother never visited. Amara had no answer she could give. What she is most afraid of is that there is no version of herself left that is capable of being a mother again.

Ernesto Villanueva is a 70-year-old widowed dentist of Colombian origin who has practiced in the same Miami clinic for nearly three decades. He came to the United States as a young man, built a quiet, ordered life, and prided himself on a steadiness that his patients and colleagues had always remarked upon. That steadiness was fractured approximately fourteen months ago when Ernesto was present at a civic ceremony in a public park — a local festival he attended every year — when a politically motivated attack unfolded without warning. Armed men in paramilitary-style clothing moved through the crowd, firing weapons and shouting directives. Ernesto was pinned behind a vendor's cart for what felt to him like an eternity, pressed against the ground, listening to shots ring out at irregular intervals, watching uniformed figures move past him with weapons raised. He was not physically wounded, but a man standing near him was struck and fell. Ernesto did not run. He stayed still, and he has never fully made peace with that fact.

In the weeks after the attack, Ernesto returned to his practice because he did not know what else to do. The clinic's routine — the hum of the suction unit, the bright overhead lights, the predictable sequencing of appointments — offered something that resembled normalcy. But the world outside the operatory had become a different place. When a car backfired on the street near his clinic, Ernesto found himself gripping the edge of the sink, unable to move for several seconds, the park flooding back through him not as a recollection but as a full sensory return: the smell of the grass, the weight of the ground beneath him, the sound of the shots as immediate and present as if they were occurring in the room. When the memory came in those moments, it did not arrive as narrative — he could not have told anyone, in ordered sentences, what had happened or in what sequence. It came as sensation, as texture, as the particular quality of light that afternoon, and it overwhelmed him so completely that he sometimes had to excuse himself from a patient mid-procedure and stand in the back hallway until the wave passed.

Ernesto had come to believe, with a certainty that felt irrefutable to him, that he should have done something more — pulled the man beside him to safety, acted rather than frozen. He returned to this conclusion repeatedly, rehearsing the moment from every angle, always arriving at the same verdict against himself. He began avoiding the evening news, because any report touching on political violence or armed groups confirmed, in his mind, that the world remained exactly as dangerous as it had been that afternoon. He started carrying a licensed firearm, which he kept in his car and sometimes in the inner pocket of his jacket, because what frightened him most was the idea of being caught without any means of response again.

At the clinic, the consequences of these changes became visible in ways Ernesto could not fully conceal. When a patient arrived wearing a security guard's uniform for an afternoon appointment, Ernesto felt his chest tighten and his attention fracture entirely. He got through the appointment by watching the man's hands. He now scans the waiting room each morning before unlocking the front door — not consciously cataloguing exits, but moving his eyes to every corner and doorway in a sweep that has become as automatic as washing his hands. He monitors his patients and his staff with a vigilance that has no clinical purpose, reading faces for signs of something he cannot name precisely but recognises immediately as threat.

A colleague gently noted that Ernesto seemed changed, and that several patients had mentioned he seemed distracted. A conversation about a recent news story involving military operations in South America left Ernesto unable to concentrate for the remainder of the afternoon. It was his daughter, calling from Bogotá, who finally said what had been unsaid — that her father did not sound like himself, and had not for over a year. Ernesto made the appointment the following week. What he most hopes for is to be able to remember what happened without being destroyed by it each time. What he fears most is that the man he was before the park no longer exists.

# Marcus

Marcus is a 34-year-old married firefighter who carries himself with the kind of quiet steadiness that comes from years of running toward danger while others run away. He is broad-shouldered and deliberate in his movements, someone who chooses his words carefully and tends to deflect personal questions with dry humor. It takes several sessions before he begins to talk about what happened in eastern Ukraine, where he spent eleven weeks as a volunteer relief worker three years ago, shortly before his marriage.

He had gone with a small NGO, helping to distribute food and medical supplies to civilian populations in contested areas. He describes the first few weeks as manageable — exhausting, frightening at times, but purposeful. He felt useful in a way that even firefighting, which he loved, had never quite given him. Then, on a Tuesday morning in late November, the convoy he was traveling with came under artillery fire on a rural road. The vehicle ahead of his was struck directly. He pulled two people from the burning wreckage. A third — a young local interpreter named Dmytro, twenty-two years old — died before Marcus could reach him. Marcus held him on the roadside in the mud and the cold while the shelling continued around them.

He came home six weeks later, thinner and quieter than he had left. His wife, Annika, noticed immediately that something had shifted in him, though he told her he was simply tired and needed time to decompress. He returned to the fire station within the month, believing that getting back to work would set things right.

Instead, the station became its own source of difficulty. The smell of burning materials, which had never troubled him before, now sends him back to that road with a visceral immediacy he cannot control. He has learned to manage his face during these moments, to keep his breathing even and his hands busy, but inside he describes it as being yanked underwater. He has started arriving early to calls so he can assess the scene before the smell reaches full intensity, a habit his crewmates have noticed and attributed to professional dedication.

At home, Marcus sleeps poorly. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, alert and certain something is wrong, and lies rigid beside Annika running through the events of the convoy attack in a loop he cannot stop. He rarely tells her when this happens. He has become protective of her in a way that has begun to feel more like distance — he monitors exits in restaurants, positions himself with his back to walls, and has quietly discouraged her from attending large public events, offering logistical excuses rather than the real reason.

He does not think of himself as someone who is struggling. He thinks of Dmytro's family, and of the two people he did pull from the wreckage, and tells himself the accounting is what it is. When asked directly how he is doing, he typically says he is fine, or that he has seen worse, or that other people had it harder. He has not told anyone at the station about the convoy. He worries, with a specificity that suggests he has thought about it at length, that his colleagues would question his composure in the field if they knew.

What has brought him in now, after three years, is a conversation with Annika that he describes only as her telling him she was losing him. He sat with that for two weeks before calling. He is not sure he believes therapy will do anything useful, and he says so plainly in the first session, though he also keeps every appointment and arrives exactly on time. There is something in him that is still trying to reach the third man on the road, still believing that if he works hard enough and stays focused, he can change what has already happened.

Vignette: Amara, Age 42

Amara came to this country seven years ago carrying almost nothing — a small bag, a borrowed phone number, and a silence she has never quite been able to explain to anyone. Before she left her home country, she had been a schoolteacher, a mother of two, a woman known in her neighborhood for her loud laugh. That version of herself feels like someone she read about once, a long time ago.

She was detained for eleven days by government forces following a protest she had attended with her brother. What happened during those eleven days — the beatings, the electric shocks applied to her hands and feet, the hours spent hooded in a stress position, the sounds of others being hurt nearby — she does not speak about in sequence. She speaks about it in fragments, when she cannot stop herself, and then she goes very quiet for the rest of the session. She says she was released only because a relative paid a bribe. She does not know what happened to two of the men who were detained with her.

She has worked for four years at a poultry processing plant on the edge of the city. The work is cold and loud and relentless, and she is grateful for it in the way that people are grateful for things that keep them too exhausted to think. She stands at her station for eight-hour shifts, moving through the same motions, and she tells herself this is manageable. Most days it is. But the smell of the plant — something metallic and organic at once — sometimes sends her somewhere else entirely. She finds herself back in that room, hands bound, heart hammering, certain she is about to die. She has learned to grip the conveyor belt rail when this happens and count backward from one hundred until the floor feels solid again. Her coworkers think she is simply quiet. She prefers it that way.

Sleep is the part of her life she dreads most. She delays it as long as she can, staying up past midnight watching videos on her phone with the brightness turned all the way down, because lying in the dark feels like being hooded again. When she does sleep, she is often back in detention — not always in the same scene, but always with the same certainty of helplessness, the same knowledge that no one is coming. She wakes with her heart slamming, sometimes shouting, and then sits on the edge of her bed for an hour, ashamed of the noise she has made in an apartment with thin walls.

Her marriage ended three years ago. Her ex-husband, also a refugee, told her she had become unreachable — that she flinched when he touched her unexpectedly, that she could not sit with her back to a door, that she left rooms without explanation and did not come back. He was not wrong. She knows she pushed him away and she knows she could not have done otherwise. Her children, now teenagers, live with her and navigate around her moods with a carefulness that breaks her heart. She sees them watching her and wonders what they understand.

She describes herself as someone who used to be curious about people and now finds them mostly exhausting and faintly threatening. She does not go to community gatherings. She does not attend her children's school events unless she can stand near an exit. She has stopped calling her sister back home because the calls make her feel the distance too acutely, and also because her sister sometimes asks questions she cannot answer.

What brings her to therapy, she says, is not the nightmares or the hypervigilance or the smell of the plant. It is that her younger son recently told her he is afraid of her — not of what she might do, but of the way she sometimes looks at him as though she does not know where she is. She says she will not let him grow up afraid of his own mother. That, she says, is the one thing she will not allow.
